points: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only; they contain no nitrogen.
Carbohydrates have hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio, the same as in water, which is why they are described as hydrated carbon.

notes.h: Classification by number of sugar units
notes.b: Carbohydrates are grouped by the number of sugar units in each molecule.
points: Monosaccharides (simple sugars) have one sugar unit: glucose, fructose and galactose, each with the formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
Disaccharides (double sugars) have two sugar units: sucrose, lactose and maltose, each with the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.
Polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates) have many sugar units joined in long chains: starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin, with the general formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ.

notes.h: Basic structure of a monosaccharide (Higher Level only)
points: A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit that cannot be split by hydrolysis into a simpler sugar.
Glucose has six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms and six oxygen atoms per molecule.
In solution, glucose forms a ring structure with hydroxyl (–OH) groups attached to the carbon atoms; these groups take part in linking sugar units together.
Fructose and galactose have the same formula as glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, but their atoms are arranged differently.
Diagram: glucose molecule drawn as a ring, with the carbon atoms numbered and the hydroxyl groups labelled.

notes.h: Formation of disaccharides and polysaccharides (Higher Level only)
points: Two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, in which one molecule of water is eliminated as the bond forms.
The bond between two sugar units is called a glycosidic link.
Glucose + glucose gives maltose; glucose + fructose gives sucrose; glucose + galactose gives lactose.
Polysaccharides form when many monosaccharide units join in the same way, with a molecule of water lost at each link.
Starch is a mixture of amylose, which has straight chains of glucose, and amylopectin, which has branched chains.
Glycogen is a highly branched polymer of glucose, the form in which animals store carbohydrate.
Cellulose has unbranched chains of glucose units held side by side by hydrogen bonds, forming strong fibres in plant cell walls.
Diagram: two glucose units joined by a glycosidic link, labelled with the water molecule released, and the resulting maltose molecule.

keyTerms.definition: A carbohydrate with one sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or galactose.
A carbohydrate formed from two monosaccharide units joined together.
A carbohydrate made of many monosaccharide units joined in long chains, such as starch or cellulose.
The bond that joins two sugar units in a disaccharide or polysaccharide.
A reaction in which two molecules join and a small molecule, usually water, is removed.
The straight-chain component of starch, made of glucose units.
The branched component of starch, made of glucose units.
A highly branched glucose polymer that is the animal storage form of carbohydrate.
One of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different atomic arrangements, such as glucose and fructose.

questions.prompt: Classify carbohydrates into three groups, giving the chemical formula and one example for each group.
questions.model: Monosaccharides: formula C₆H₁₂O₆, example glucose (or fructose or galactose). Disaccharides: formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, example sucrose (or lactose or maltose). Polysaccharides: formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ, example starch (or glycogen, cellulose or pectin). Each group is defined by the number of sugar units it contains.

questions.prompt: Describe the basic chemical structure of a monosaccharide, explain how a disaccharide and a polysaccharide are formed, and give one example of each.
questions.model: A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit with the formula C₆H₁₂O₆; glucose has six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen atoms and forms a ring in solution with hydroxyl groups. A disaccharide forms when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, eliminating one molecule of water and creating a glycosidic link; example: sucrose from glucose and fructose, formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. A polysaccharide forms when many monosaccharide units join in the same way, with water lost at each link; example: starch, made of amylose and amylopectin chains. Marks are for the monosaccharide structure, the condensation reaction with water lost, and a named example of each class.
